1:
Ellicott reads this opening almost entirely as a comparison with the parallel in Kings, and the comparison turns out to carry a judgement. The chronicler omits the verse which relates the call of Jeroboam to the throne of Israel, and gives the muster in a slightly abridged form, using a different word for the kingdom and the longer form of the prophet's name. More tellingly, where Kings has the house of Judah and Benjamin and the remnant of the people, the chronicler writes all Israel in Judah and Benjamin; Ellicott allows this may be a mere abbreviation, since the house of Judah and Benjamin was the remnant of Israel that continued loyal to David, but he thinks there may be a hint that Judah and Benjamin were the true Israel and the apostate North had forfeited its right to that honourable name, while others suppose a reference to northern tribesmen living in the southern territory. He notes the Syriac reads the clause differently again and the Greek gives simply all Judah and Benjamin. On the royal title he is firmest: by the significant expression king of Judah, accomplished facts receive at the outset the seal of divine assent.

Two of Ellicott's smaller notes bear on how carefully the chronicler worked. Where the prophecy is reported, Kings adds a phrase which produces a tautology, and the chronicler has avoided it; and where Kings and the versions have the singular word, which Ellicott thinks is no doubt right since that is the usual phrase, this text has the plural. He would render the reason given for the prohibition literally, that from me arose this matter, meaning the revolt of the ten tribes, and compares the statement in the previous chapter that the cause was of God. He also records a fact about the chapter as a whole which has nothing to do with the chronicler at all: the remainder of it is wanting in the Syriac and Arabic versions, which substitute a run of material out of Kings instead and then break off abruptly without finishing the prophecy of Ahijah.

Henry takes the same four verses as a study in three characters successively assumed. Rehoboam acts first like a bold man, raising an army to reduce the revolters, with Judah and Benjamin not merely resolved to continue their allegiance but ready to give the best assistance they could for the recovery of his right, Judah being his own tribe and Benjamin the tribe in which the greater part of Jerusalem stood. Then he acts like a conscientious man, letting the design fall when God forbade it, either because he reverenced the divine authority or because he knew that going against the command he would not prosper but risk losing what he still had; and Henry draws the rule, that it is dangerous to undertake anything contrary to the will of God, but especially a war. He notices that God addresses him as the son of Solomon, which he takes to intimate that the loss was determined for Solomon's sin and that it would be to no purpose to oppose a decree already gone forth; and that they obeyed although it looked mean and would turn to their reproach among their neighbours. Last Rehoboam acts like a discreet man, seeing it was to no purpose to think of reducing those who had revolted, and fortifying his own country instead. Henry's comment on that reversal is the sharpest thing in the passage: a few good words might have prevented the defection, but now all the forces of his kingdom cannot bring them back. Delitzsch gives the sequence plainly: Rehoboam wished to compel the ten tribes by arms to submit again and levied all the men capable of bearing arms in the two tribes, until the prophet commanded him in the name of the Lord to desist.
5:
What Rehoboam was fortifying against is the real question here, and the list of names answers it if you plot it. Ellicott does so and reaches a conclusion that cuts against the obvious reading: of the fifteen fortified cities enumerated, all but two lay south and west of Jerusalem, so that Rehoboam appears to have been more afraid of an attack from the south and west, that is from the Egyptians, than of a war with the northern kingdom. The two exceptions, Zorah and Aijalon, lay farthest north, and Ellicott suggests they may have become Benjamite cities at the epoch of the migration of Dan. Clarke reads the same list the other way and without hesitation, holding that Rehoboam was obliged to strengthen his frontiers against the encroachments of the men of Israel, and noting that Jeroboam did the same thing on his part to prevent inroads from Judah. Delitzsch takes no view of the strategy but closes the account where the list closes, observing that the final clause about Judah and Benjamin belonging to him answers the statement in the previous chapter that Israel had revolted from the house of David, and so rounds off the record of everything Rehoboam did to establish his power and consolidate his kingdom.

On the identity of the places the commentators are candid about how little is settled. Delitzsch says of Gath that it was a royal city of the Philistines, first made subject to the Israelites by David and under Solomon the seat of its own king who was himself subject to the Israelite king, and that it has not yet been certainly discovered. Gill will not have it a Philistine city at all, holding that this cannot be the Gath which was one of the principalities of the Philistines but a city in the tribe of Judah, of which we nowhere else read, unless it is the same as the Gath compounded with another name elsewhere. Ellicott leaves it uncertain and offers only a possible valley north of Ascalon. On Adullam, Delitzsch reports that it has not yet been discovered, rejects one conjecture as hardly correct, and thinks it much more probable that its site was a place now called Deir Dubban; Ellicott proposes a different candidate again. Adoraim both treat as the better attested name, Ellicott noting that it appears in a later historical book and often in Josephus in connection with Mareshah, and that it is not found elsewhere in the Old Testament, while Delitzsch adds from Josephus that it was taken by Hyrcanus and rebuilt by Gabinius under another name.

On what fortifying actually meant the two work in close agreement. Ellicott renders the verb literally as strengthened, that is, put into an efficient condition for defence by providing commandants and stores of arms and food, and notes that the word the chronicler uses for the strongholds is peculiar to him, as is the form of words rendered made them exceeding strong. He also glosses the word for captains as leaders or princes, meaning here commandants, and identifies the shields with the targets mentioned earlier in the book. Delitzsch gives the same account in the same order, that Rehoboam increased the strength of the fortresses by placing them in a thoroughly efficient condition to defend themselves against attack, appointing commandants, provisioning them and laying up stores of all kinds of arms. Clarke adds the one point neither of them makes, and it is a point about purpose rather than method: the stores of provisions were laid up not only to enable the cities to endure a siege but also so that they might be able, from their situation, to supply desolate places. Ellicott closes the section by reading the last clause as a definition of Rehoboam's territory, and would render it literally that there fell to him Judah and Benjamin.
13:
Why the priests and Levites left is explained the same way by all, and Henry most fully. Jeroboam cast them off, he says, by setting up a way of worship they could not in conscience comply with while forbidding them to go up to Jerusalem, so that he totally cast them off from executing the priest's office; and he was very willing they should turn themselves out, to make room for the mean and scandalous persons he ordained for the high places. No marvel, Henry adds, if he that cast off God cast off his ministers, since they would not serve his gods nor worship his image. He then gives three reasons why the Levites abandoned cities in which their maintenance had seemed well settled: they could do no good among neighbours in whom the old proneness to idolatry had revived; they would be under continual temptation to base compliances and in danger of being drawn insensibly into evil; and if they kept their integrity they had reason to expect persecution. Clarke gives the political motive, that Jeroboam feared the priests would turn the hearts of the people to the true God and then they would revolt to Judah, and therefore established a new worship and made new gods.

On what that worship actually was Ellicott and Clarke each add something the other does not. Ellicott reads it as deliberate policy: Jeroboam established two centres of worship within his own dominions so that his subjects might cease to visit the temple, and in appointing priests chosen promiscuously from all classes he struck a direct blow at the Levitical order. Such local sanctuaries existed not only at the two famous centres, he notes, but in other cities of the north; and he makes the chapter's sharpest claim about the calves: since they represented the God of Israel, it appears Jeroboam encouraged a system of syncretism, or mixture of worships. On the word rendered devils he gives satyrs, literally goats, indicating a prevalence of debasing idolatry. Clarke supplies the reason Ellicott leaves out: as the golden calves were in imitation of the Egyptian ox-god, so divine honours were no doubt paid to the goat, which was an object of religious veneration in Egypt. On the phrase about Jeroboam's sons Ellicott takes it, with Keil, for his successors on the throne, since in this matter all the kings of Israel walked in his footsteps, and observes that of his own sons only Nadab ever reigned.

The three years of faithfulness draw a defence of the record and two reckonings of what followed. Ellicott quotes Bertheau that there is no ground for suspecting the antiquity of this record, since it is antecedently probable that pressure from the north occasioned a proportionally greater earnestness in the religious life of the south, and that the north was weakened and the south strengthened by the migration; he adds that this also explains Jeroboam's abstention from molesting his rival's territory, which bears on where Rehoboam built his forts. He takes walking in the way of David and Solomon to mean serving the Lord according to the system those monarchs enacted, and notes drily that the countenance Solomon in his old age gave to foreign religions is here again ignored by the chronicler. Clarke counts the years on the other side of that boundary: during the three Rehoboam prospered, but for fourteen years after he and the people were unfaithful, except at such intervals as the hand of God's judgments was upon them. On the migration itself Clarke reckons the gains, that all the truly pious joined him out of every tribe and the whole tribe of Levi, deprived of its functions, joined him too, so that he had Judah, Benjamin and Levi and probably part of Simeon; Ellicott notes only that they came to sacrifice and settle, and that similar migrations are recorded in two later reigns.
18:
Whether Rehoboam broke the law of the firstborn in preferring Abijah is the one point where the commentary squarely divides. Clarke says he did: Abijah certainly was not the firstborn, but as Rehoboam loved Maachah more than any of his wives he preferred her son, probably through his mother's influence; this sort of preference is forbidden in Deuteronomy, though he had a sort of precedent in David's preference for Solomon. Ellicott denies the infringement outright, naming the commentary that alleged it, on the ground that the right of the firstborn was only a double share of a man's property and not the succession, and he adds a precedent of his own from Solomon's accession. He would render the appointment more exactly as making Abijah head, that is prince, among his brethren, and takes the brief phrase that follows to give the reason, for making him king. Henry reads the dispersal of the other sons as the same policy from the other end, either that they might not be rivals to the son designed for the succession, or rather because Rehoboam could repose confidence in them for preserving the public peace, trusting them with fenced cities he had taken care to victual. He calls it after-wisdom, better than none, though dearly bought with the loss of a kingdom. Clarke makes the motive defensive: it was true policy to disperse his sons through the provinces, since they were not likely to league with Jeroboam against their father.

Ellicott's textual work on the genealogy is the chapter's most careful. The reading daughter rather than son is right, on the authority of the Greek and Latin and many Hebrew manuscripts. Jerimoth does not occur in the list of David's sons unless the name is a corruption of Ithream, so he was probably one of the sons of the concubines. The conjunction before Abihail is absent from the present Hebrew but supplied by the Greek, and the meaning is probably that both of Mahalath's parents are named; the Greek and Latin instead make Abihail a second wife, but the construction and the following verses make it evident that only one wife is mentioned, and a daughter of David's eldest brother could hardly become the wife of David's grandson. Maachah, called the daughter of Absalom, must be his granddaughter, since Tamar is named elsewhere as Absalom's one daughter, and Josephus makes Maachah Tamar's daughter. Even the number of concubines he doubts, since Josephus gives thirty and the difference in Hebrew is one letter, while the recurrence of the same number in the count of daughters is also suspicious.

On the marriages the moral reckonings diverge in degree rather than kind. Clarke calls eighteen wives and sixty concubines bad enough but not so abandoned as his father, counts the issue at eighty-eight children, and observes that to the education of the whole Rehoboam could pay little attention, since numerous families are often neglected and children by different women must be worse off still. He grants that Rehoboam was much addicted to women, yet notes that we do not find he formed any heathenish alliances of this kind, and supposes he strengthened his political connections by these means. Henry turns the same comparison into two advantages: Rehoboam was wiser than his father in that he does not appear to have married strange wives, those named here being not only daughters of Israel but of the family of David, and happier in having many sons and daughters where we read of only one son of Solomon's. Clarke adds a tradition that bears on how she is named elsewhere: the Targum explains that because she was upright her name was changed to the more excellent Michaiah and her father's to Uriel, that the name of Absalom might not be remembered. Ellicott offers the plainer explanation of why she was loved: she probably inherited her mother's and grandfather's beauty.
